2.title: Living Stones and Holy Exiles: Identity, Witness, and the Suffering Christ
2.overview:
Chapter 2 moves from who Christians are (vv. 1–10) to how they live in a hostile world (vv. 11–25). Identity produces conduct, and conduct commends the identity.

The chapter ends with Christ’s unjust suffering (vv. 18–25). Submission there is following the suffering Servant, who bore our sins.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Living Stones, a Royal Priesthood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter tells the newborn people of God what they are: hungry for the word, built on Christ the living stone into one house and priesthood, and given every title Israel was given at Sinai.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priesthood of All Believers

Coming to Christ, the living stone, believers are built into one spiritual house and a holy priesthood, offering sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel’s titles were given to Gentile converts with no status at all.

Now: Once not a people, now God’s people; once without mercy, now shown mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: So put away all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander. Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation— if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Peter 2 tells God’s new people who they are and how to live in a hostile world: craving the word (vv. 1–3), built on Christ the living stone into a spiritual house and priesthood (vv. 4–10), and living as exiles whose good lives silence slander, under authorities and harsh masters (vv. 11–20), because Christ suffered for them and bore their sins (vv. 21–25).

So put away all malice. Because you have been born again (1:22–23), strip it off like clothing (James 1:21): these are the garments of the old family, and they no longer fit. Malice is ill will, the inner wickedness from which the rest grows.

Deceit, hypocrisy, envy, slander. The five items have one thing in common. Every one is a sin against other people, and four of the five are done with words or with a face. Peter has just commanded earnest love from a pure heart (1:22); this is the list of what makes that impossible. Deceit, dolos, is guile, trickery, the bait on a hook that hides the barb. Hypocrisy, hypokrisis, is the actor’s mask, set deliberately beside the sincere, un-masked love of 1:22, which is the same word negated. Envy, phthonos, is the resentment of another’s good. And slander, katalalia, evil speaking, backbiting (James 4:11), was exactly what these readers were suffering from outside (2:12). Peter will not let a congregation being slandered do to each other what is being done to them. And note the word all, three times. A church cannot have a little backbiting.

Pure spiritual milk. The image follows the birth: newly born people should have an appetite. Newborn infants, artigennēta brephē, are babies just born, and long for, epipothēsate, is a strong verb: crave, yearn for intensely. It is the noise a hungry baby makes, which is not a polite request. A newborn does not want milk among other things; it wants milk with its whole body, and it will not be distracted by a rattle. Spiritual, logikon, is related to logos, word, and here it very probably points to the word that gave them birth (1:23–25). And pure, adolon, is a play on the deceit, dolon, of verse 1: guileless, unadulterated, nothing mixed in. Put off the deceit; drink the milk with no deceit in it.

Grow up into salvation. Elsewhere milk is the beginner’s diet (Hebrews 5:12–13); here it is the food that produces growth, and the diet does not change. The oldest saint is as dependent on the word as the newest convert, and should be as hungry.

Tasted that the Lord is good. This quotes Psalm 34:8: oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! It is a psalm Peter draws on repeatedly in this letter (3:10–12). Tasted, egeusasthe, means experienced. And the Lord in Psalm 34 is the LORD, Yahweh; here Peter applies it to Christ, the living stone of the next verse. He does it without comment, as though it were obvious that the LORD of David’s psalm is Jesus. And good, chrēstos, kind, gracious, sounds almost exactly like Christos in Greek. Peter may well intend the echo: you have tasted that the Lord is kind; you have tasted Christ. The argument is from experience: an appetite follows a taste. People who have genuinely tasted something good do not need to be persuaded to want more of it.

What if I have no appetite for the Bible? Then do what a doctor would tell you to do with a child who has stopped eating: look for what is spoiling the appetite, and keep offering the food. Peter puts the two together: put away malice, deceit, envy and slander, and crave the milk. Unconfessed sin, a grudge, or a diet of constant distraction will kill spiritual hunger. Confess them. Then read a little, regularly, and ask God before you open it to show you Christ there. Read the Gospels if the rest is hard. Appetite often returns by eating; and the God who caused you to be born again is the one who gives his children hunger.

How do I actually put off slander and envy? By naming them honestly, and by replacing them. Catch yourself when you start the sentence that begins, have you heard about…, and stop it. When someone in your church is praised and something in you shrinks, recognise it as envy and thank God aloud for the person instead. Ask whether what you are about to say would be said if the person were in the room. If there is a real grievance, take it to the person, not to others (Matthew 18:15). And remember that you are stripping off old clothes because you have new ones: Christ’s love for you leaves no need to diminish anyone else.

For worship. He is good and kind, and we have tasted it: the day we first understood that the blood of Christ was for us, and every time his word lands on a weary heart like milk on a hungry child. The LORD whom David tasted as a fugitive has a name now: Jesus, whose kindness we taste at his table and will taste at his feast for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious, you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As you come to him. The metaphor changes from infancy to masonry. Come is the word for drawing near to God in worship (Hebrews 4:16), and the tense is present: keep coming, morning by morning, Sunday by Sunday.

A living stone rejected by men. The phrase is a deliberate paradox. Stone is the deadest material there is, and Peter attaches the word he has been using of hope (1:3) and of the word of God (1:23). A stone that is alive, because it has been raised from the dead. Rejected, apodedokimasmenon, is a technical word: tested and rejected, declared unfit after examination. It comes from Psalm 118:22. Builders inspected stones before using them, and set aside the ones that would not do. The religious leaders examined Jesus, cross-questioned him, put him on trial, and threw him out (Mark 8:31; 12:10).

Chosen and precious. From Isaiah 28:16, applied first to Christ: two verdicts on the same person. Men rejected him; God chose and honoured him. The readers, rejected in Pontus, are being told which verdict counts.

You yourselves like living stones. Peter’s name means rock, and if anyone could have claimed to be the foundation stone, it was him. He does not. Christ is the living stone, and Peter is one stone among many: the slave and the apostle alike.

A spiritual house. The passive matters: they are being built, oikodomeisthe, and the present tense says God is still at work on it. Not building themselves, and not assembling by choice. Someone is doing it. And the singular is the point. Not houses but a house, one structure. A spiritual house, oikos pneumatikos, is a temple made of people and indwelt by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:20–22; 1 Corinthians 3:16). The temple in Jerusalem was made of dead stones and would soon be thrown down. God’s new temple is made of living people, and it will never fall. A stone on its own is rubble; it becomes masonry only by being set against other stones. Peter is writing to scattered, isolated believers and telling them they are load-bearing parts of one building.

The quarry and the chisel. A stone is cut out of the rock, shaped until it fits, and set next to stones it did not choose. Every Christian knows something of all three. The Builder is not making a pile of separate statues but a house for himself to live in.

To be a holy priesthood. Not some believers, but all: the root of what the Reformers called the priesthood of all believers. In the temple ordinary Israelites stood in the outer courts while the priests went in. Peter says the congregation is the building, is the priesthood, and offers the sacrifices (Revelation 1:6).

Spiritual sacrifices. Not animals, but praise and thanksgiving, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name (Hebrews 13:15); doing good and sharing what we have (Hebrews 13:16); our bodies given to God as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1); gifts for the gospel (Philippians 4:18); prayer (Revelation 8:3–4); and declaring his excellencies (v. 9). Acceptable, euprosdektous, means well-pleasing. And the last three words keep it from being self-important: acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. Even the offerings of a priesthood need a mediator. Our praise is stained and our good works are mixed; not one of them is perfect. But Christ offered God a perfect obedience in our place, and so God receives our offerings gladly, because they come to him through the hands of his Son, our one great High Priest.

Where Christians differ: is there a special priesthood in the church? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches maintain an ordained priesthood that offers sacrifice on behalf of the people. This commentary’s view: The New Testament teaches the priesthood of all believers. Every Christian is a priest, offering spiritual sacrifices directly to God through Christ, the one great High Priest. The church has elders and deacons, who lead and serve, but no priestly caste that mediates between God and the people (1 Timothy 2:5). Peter himself, the first leader of the apostles, describes himself as a fellow elder (5:1), and Christ, not Peter, as the stone on which the church is built.

If every believer is a priest, is there any place for ordained ministers? Every believer has direct access to God through Christ and offers spiritual sacrifices; there is no need for a priestly class to offer sacrifices for others, as in the Roman Mass. But the New Testament still gives elders to teach and shepherd the church (5:1–4). They are not priests between God and his people, but servants of the word among a priestly people.

Can I be a Christian without a church? Peter’s picture says no, not in any healthy sense. A living stone is not meant to lie in a field. Christ saves individuals, but he saves them into a house, and the New Testament knows nothing of believers who refuse to belong to a local congregation. If you have been hurt by a church, that is real and grievous, and you may need time and care. But the answer is a better church, not no church. Find a congregation that preaches Christ faithfully, commit to it, and let yourself be set in the wall, rough edges and all.

On a Tuesday. You are a priest today, wherever you are. The sink, the desk, the hospital ward and the steering wheel are altars. Offer your praise aloud in the car. Offer your work as done for him. Offer a gift to someone in need.

verseByVerse.quote: For it stands in Scripture: "Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." So the honor is for you who believe, but for those who do not believe, "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone," and "A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense." They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it stands in Scripture. Peter stacks three stone texts, and the effect is cumulative: the rejection of Jesus was not a surprise the apostles had to explain away. It was written.

A cornerstone. Isaiah 28:16. The cornerstone set the lines of the whole building; every wall was measured from it. In Isaiah’s day Jerusalem trusted alliances with Egypt; God says, I am laying a stone of my own.

Not put to shame. In the Greek of Isaiah the stone is a person: whoever believes in him (Romans 9:33). Their neighbours were shaming them. God promised that the shame would not stick.

The honor. To you who believe he is precious, and the honour that is his is given to you. The people the world dishonours are joined to the stone God honours.

The stone the builders rejected. The second text is Psalm 118:22. The Lord had quoted it of himself (Matthew 21:42), and Peter had quoted it before the Sanhedrin to the very builders who had done the rejecting: this Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone (Acts 4:11). He has been preaching this text for some thirty years. The builders, the religious leaders, rejected him, but God made him the chief stone. Unbelief cannot overturn God’s choice. They can throw the stone out of the building site; God puts it back at the corner.

A stone of stumbling. The third text is Isaiah 8:14, and here the images collide deliberately. Stumbling, proskomma, and offence, skandalon, a trap, a snare, a cause of falling. The same stone is a foundation to some and an obstacle to others. Nothing about the stone changes; what differs is whether a man builds on it or trips over it. For unbelievers Christ is not a foundation but an obstacle, and they fall over him to their ruin (1 Corinthians 1:23). And no one can simply walk past this stone. It is set in the middle of the road of every human life. You will either build on Christ or fall over him.

Is it presumptuous to say everyone must either build on Christ or fall over him? Only if Christians had invented the claim or thought themselves better for believing it. But the claim is Christ’s, not ours (John 14:6), and the people who make it are those who once tripped over him themselves and were picked up by mercy. Every view of the world says some people are wrong; the question is whether it is true. And this stone is not placed to exclude anyone. It is laid in Zion for whoever believes, Jew or Gentile, respectable or ruined, and the only people kept out are those who refuse to build. A narrow door is not arrogant if it is the only door and stands open.

They stumble because they disobey the word. Disobey means refuse to be persuaded: the gospel is a command to repent and believe. Peter gives the reason for the stumbling first, and it is a real refusal, genuinely theirs.

As they were destined to do. God appointed that those who disobey would stumble: their own guilty choice, within his sovereign purpose. Peter does not soften either half, and he does not make God the author of the disobedience.

Where Christians differ: does God destine people to unbelief? Some read this as teaching only that God appointed the consequence (stumbling) for those who freely choose to disobey. This commentary’s view: The verse teaches that those who disobey stumble according to God’s appointment. God is sovereign over all things, including the rejection of Christ by unbelievers (Romans 9:18–22; Acts 4:27–28). Yet the stumbling is caused by their own disobedience, for which they are wholly responsible. God passes over some, leaving them in their sin, and justly appoints them to its consequences; he does not create unbelief in an innocent heart. The doctrine is to be handled with humility and reverence, not speculation, and it is set against the glory of the chosen in the next verse.

Does as they were destined to do mean that God destined some to disobey? Within the Reformed tradition some read it to mean that God appointed the stumbling as the consequence of disobedience: those who reject Christ are destined to stumble over him. Others read it more strongly: their disobedience itself fell within God’s purpose, as the verdict above holds. Either way, their stumbling is their own act, because they disobey the word, and God’s purpose stands behind it. No one in hell will be able to say that he wanted Christ and was refused.

Should this make me worry that I or someone I love is destined to stumble? No. This verse is not given to make anyone examine God’s secret decree; it is given to explain why so many reject Christ, and to steady believers who are puzzled by it. If you are worried about whether you will stumble over Christ, the answer is simple: come to him now. Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame. And for those you love who are stumbling, keep praying and keep speaking. You do not know who is chosen. Saul of Tarsus stumbled over this stone for years, and then was knocked down by it on the Damascus road and rose up a believer.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself honestly where Christ still offends you: a command, a doctrine, a claim that embarrasses you in front of friends. That is where you are tempted to stumble rather than build. Bring it to him.

verseByVerse.quote: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you are a chosen race. But you: and the contrast with the stumblers is total. Four titles follow, and every one is lifted straight out of what God said to Israel, most of it at Sinai (Exodus 19:5–6; Deuteronomy 7:6; Isaiah 43:20–21). A chosen race, genos eklekton, is from Isaiah 43:20: a new people, not by physical descent but by God’s choice. Consider what it would have meant to hear that read aloud. Many of these were people of little account: no priesthood, no nation of their own to boast of, and few possessions. Peter tells them they are all four. And every title belonged first to Christ. He is the chosen one, the stone God chose (v. 4); he is the King who is also Priest; he is the Holy One of God; he is the beloved Son in whom the Father delights. These people are chosen because they are in the Chosen One, and everything God says of them he first said of him.

A royal priesthood. From Exodus 19:6: you shall be to me a kingdom of priests. Royal priesthood, basileion hierateuma: priests who belong to the King, and who share his reign (Revelation 1:6; 5:10). In Israel kings and priests were kept strictly apart; when King Uzziah tried to burn incense in the temple, he was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). The one clear figure in the Old Testament who was both is the mysterious Melchizedek (Genesis 14:18), and the Messiah was promised to be a priest for ever after his order (Psalm 110:4). Christ is that King-Priest, and in him his people are both too.

A holy nation. A nation without borders, army or earthly capital, drawn from every nation, and the only one that will last for ever.

A people for his own possession. The Hebrew behind it, segullah (Exodus 19:5), was used of a king’s private treasure (1 Chronicles 29:3). People whom Rome counted as nobody are the crown jewels of the King of heaven.

Proclaim the excellencies. Tell out loud his mighty deeds (Isaiah 43:21). The whole congregation is given the priest’s job: not chiefly to have an identity, but to point at someone else’s.

Marvelous light. Called, kalesantos: God’s effectual call, which means not merely an invitation that might be refused but the summons that actually brings a person to life and faith, as Jesus’ call brought Lazarus out of the tomb (John 11:43). Darkness: ignorance, sin, the realm of Satan (Acts 26:18; Colossians 1:13). Marvellous light, thaumaston phōs: wonderful light, the light of God’s truth and presence. A conversion described as a relocation, a total transfer, and it echoes the exodus again: out of Egypt, through the darkness of the plague, and into the land. And the light is marvellous, which means it never stops being surprising. Christians who have walked in it for fifty years are still astonished.

Not a people. Hosea named his children Not My People and No Mercy, and God promised to reverse the names (Hosea 1:6–10; 2:23). Peter, like Paul (Romans 9:25–26), applies the reversal to Gentiles who never had the names in the first place.

Now mercy. Whatever these readers are being called in Pontus, their name has already been changed once, and the God who changed it does not change it back.

Where Christians differ: is the church a replacement for Israel, or are they two separate peoples? Dispensationalists (Christians who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras, and who expect God to fulfil his promises to ethnic Israel separately from the church) keep Israel and the church as two distinct peoples with distinct promises; some speak of replacement theology, in which the church replaces Israel entirely. This commentary’s view: Peter applies Israel’s titles directly to the mostly Gentile church. The church is not a separate people from Israel but the fulfilment of God’s purpose for Israel: one people of God, Jew and Gentile together in Christ, the true seed of Abraham (Galatians 3:29; Ephesians 2:11–22; Romans 11:17–24). This is fulfilment, not mere replacement: believing Jews were the core of the church, and God continues to graft Jews back in through faith in Christ (Romans 11:23–26).

Has the church replaced Israel? Peter applies Israel’s titles to the church, Jew and Gentile together, because the church shares Israel’s calling as the one people of God in Christ (Exodus 19:5–6; Ephesians 2:11–22). That does not mean that the Jewish people have no place in God’s purposes; Paul still expects many to be grafted back in (Romans 11:23–26), and Christians differ on how and when that will happen. It means that there is one people of God, and its centre is Christ.

I struggle with low self-worth. How does this help? It gives you a name that does not depend on how you feel, what others say, or how well you have done this week. God calls you chosen, royal, holy, treasured, and he says it to people who were once nobody. Your worth is not something you have to build; it is something he has declared and paid for. That does not make you better than anyone else, because all of it is mercy. But it does mean that the voices calling you worthless are lying. When they speak, answer with God’s words: once I was not a people, now I am God’s people; once I had not received mercy, now I have.

How do I proclaim his excellencies if I am not a preacher? By speaking of what God has done for you, naturally and honestly, in the ordinary conversations of life. Tell a friend what you are thankful for and why. Explain, when someone asks why you are different, what Christ means to you. Sing in church as if you meant it. Pray aloud with a struggling neighbour. Live in such a way that people ask (3:15). The excellencies of God are not a script for professionals; they are the testimony of everyone who has been brought out of darkness and can still remember what it was like.

For worship. He looked on people who were not a people, and made them his people; on those who had no mercy, and gave them mercy. Chosen, royal, holy, treasured: every title is a gift, every gift is mercy, and every mercy was bought with blood.
verseByVerse.note: Titles once given to Israel at Sinai are now given to the church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–25 — Submission, and the Steps of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now Peter turns to how exiles live among neighbours who slander them: holiness within, goodness without, and willing submission for the Lord’s sake, first to rulers and then, for slaves, to masters. The ground of it all is Christ, who suffered unjustly and bore our sins.
verseByVerse.theology:
Entrusting Rather Than Suppressing

Christ did not revile in return; he kept entrusting himself to the one who judges justly. Then he did what no follower can copy: he bore our sins in his body on the tree.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter spoke directly to slaves, and told believers to honour an emperor who would soon persecute them.

Now: Follow in his steps: do good, refuse revenge (which never means staying in danger), and hand the case to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul. Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, I urge you. Peter does not lecture strangers; he pleads with people he loves. Sojourners and exiles, the words of 1:1 and 1:17, now ground the ethics: you do not belong here, so do not live like those who do.

Abstain. Keep away from, hold yourself back. Passions of the flesh are the desires of fallen human nature turned in on itself (Galatians 5:19–21), not the body, which God made and will raise.

Wage war. To campaign as soldiers (James 4:1). Peter has spent two chapters on what the neighbours are doing; here he names a nearer enemy, inside the walls, campaigning against the very soul whose salvation he has described (1:9). Lust always presents itself as a friend. Peter tears the uniform off.

Among the Gentiles. Here unbelievers: Peter has so thoroughly reclassified his Gentile readers as Israel that their old category is now the outsiders’ name. Honourable means good, beautiful: not merely correct but winsome.

As evildoers. When, not if. The slander is assumed. Speak against, katalalousin, is the slander word from verse 1. Early Christians were accused of atheism, because they rejected the gods and had no images; of cannibalism, because rumours of eating someone’s body and drinking his blood leaked out from the Lord’s Supper; of incest, because they called each other brother and sister and greeted with a kiss; and of disloyalty to Rome, because they would not worship the emperor. They were bad for business too. Fifty years after this letter, Pliny, governor of these very provinces of Bithynia and Pontus, wrote to the emperor Trajan that, with the spread of the Christians, the temples had been almost deserted and buyers for sacrificial meat had grown scarce, until his measures revived them. He tortured two slave women, whom the Christians called deaconesses, and found nothing but what he called a perverse and excessive superstition. He also reported that the Christians bound themselves by oath not to steal, commit adultery or break their word. Something like Peter’s strategy can be seen at work: even the persecutor found no evidence for the worst of the slanders. And the slander had been aimed at their Lord first. The charge his accusers brought to Pilate was that he was doing evil (John 18:30); he was condemned as an evildoer, and hung between two of them, and his life was the evidence that answered the charge.

Your good deeds. See means watch over time: the slow watching of neighbours trying to find something wrong. The strategy is not argument but visibility, as the Lord said on the hillside: let your light shine before others (Matthew 5:16).

What is the day of visitation? A day when God comes, hēmera episkopēs, whether to save (Luke 19:44) or to judge (Isaiah 10:3). Some read it as the day of judgement, when even unbelievers will be forced to acknowledge that God’s people were right; the more likely reading is that pagans who have watched Christians’ good deeds will themselves be converted and glorify God when he visits them in mercy. So good lives can win slanderers to Christ.

How do I fight a desire that feels overwhelming? Treat it as Peter does: as an enemy, not a part of you to be negotiated with. Abstain means keep away, so do not stand near the fire: remove the apps, change the route, avoid being alone with the bottle or the person. Tell a trusted Christian friend, because sin grows in the dark and shrinks in the light. When the desire comes, turn your mind to Christ and to what is promised (1:13); a greater love expels a lesser one. And when you fall, do not give up the war; confess, receive forgiveness, and get back up. The soldier who falls is not the one who loses. The one who changes sides is.

What if people speak badly of me even though I am doing good? Then you are in good company, and Peter has written this letter for you. Keep doing good, without bitterness. Do not spend your energy defending your reputation; let your life do the talking over time. If a specific accusation is false, you may correct it calmly. But leave the verdict to God, who sees, and to the slow work of evidence. Many people who slandered Christians in one decade were Christians in the next. Your patience may be the thing God uses to bring them to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution, whether it be to the emperor as supreme, or to governors as sent by him to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good. For this is the will of God, that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be subject for the Lord’s sake. To be subject is to take your place willingly in an order God has made (2:13, 18; 3:1), here the order of law and government (Romans 13:1–7). “For the Lord’s sake” gives the reason and the limit. The reason: not because every official deserves it, nor merely to avoid being caught, but because the Lord who ransomed us asks it, and because law-abiding Christians make the gospel believable (v. 15). He himself submitted to a corrupt high priest’s court and to Pilate’s, for his Father’s sake. The limit: what is done for the Lord’s sake can never include what the Lord forbids. When the authorities ordered the apostles to stop preaching, Peter answered, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). In practice: pay your taxes, keep the speed limit, speak of leaders with respect even when you vote against them, and refuse only where obeying would mean sin, openly and accepting the cost.

To every human institution. Government is human in its forms, monarchy or parliament, but ordained by God in its existence (Romans 13:1).

The emperor as supreme. Emperor, basileus, king. Supreme, hyperechonti, highest authority. Remember who the emperor was. This letter was most likely written in the early 60s, which means the man as supreme was Nero, who within a few years would be using Christians as living torches in his gardens, as the Roman historian Tacitus records, and under whom, according to early tradition, Peter himself would die. That fact should govern how the verse is read. Peter is not describing an ideal government or making submission conditional on good behaviour. He is telling a persecuted minority to be model subjects of a ruler who will kill them. And the governors sent by him were men like Pilate, Felix and Festus, and later Pliny in Bithynia. Peter knew such men: a governor had sent his Lord to the cross.

To punish and to praise. The stated function is justice (Romans 13:3–4), and Peter, flogged by the council (Acts 5:40), states it anyway: he describes the office rather than flattering the officeholders. A world with corrupt police is still safer than a world with none.

Put to silence. Muzzle, as one muzzles an ox. The best answer to slander is a life that makes it obviously untrue: not winning the argument but removing its material.

Where Christians differ: when may Christians disobey the government? This commentary’s view: Christians must submit to governing authorities as a general rule, paying taxes, obeying laws and honouring officials (Romans 13:1–7). But when the government commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, believers must obey God rather than men (Acts 4:19–20; 5:29; Daniel 3; 6). Even then, they should accept the consequences peacefully, without violent rebellion, as Peter and the apostles did. Christians may also work through lawful means to change unjust laws.

The apostle who disobeyed. Peter knew the limits: it was he who told the Sanhedrin, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), and took the beating rejoicing (Acts 5:41). The pattern is Daniel at his open window: respectful, unbending, and willing to pay.

What about a government I believe is wicked? Peter’s readers had one, and his instruction did not change. You may disagree with your rulers, vote against them, protest lawfully and speak the truth about them. You must still pray for them (1 Timothy 2:1–2), pay your taxes, obey just laws and refuse to speak of them with contempt. The limit is not whether you like them, but whether they command you to sin. Where they do, you obey God, openly and peaceably, and accept the cost. A Christian’s politics should be marked by more respect, more prayer and less rage than his neighbour’s, because he knows who is really on the throne.

For worship. Nero had his day, and his gardens are dust, and the Lord he persecuted reigns, King of kings. We can submit to earthly rulers without fear because they are not the last authority, and defy them without hatred when we must, because their power was given from above.
verseByVerse.note: The emperor at the time was probably Nero.

verseByVerse.quote: Live as people who are free, not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil, but living as servants of God. Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Live as people who are free. An extraordinary thing to say to people told to submit to Nero, and to slaves two verses later. Peter’s freedom is not political: free from sin’s slavery, the law’s condemnation, and the fear of man and of death (John 8:36; Galatians 5:1).

A cover-up for evil. A veil thrown over what is underneath: liberty in Christ invoked as permission (Galatians 5:13). A freedom used to do evil has already become a new slavery.

Servants of God. Free, and slaves, and the paradox is the resolution (Romans 6:22). A man wholly owned by God is beyond the reach of anyone else’s ownership, which is why a Christian slave in verse 18 can be told he is free. A fish is free in water, not out of it.

The sons are free. Peter had learned this freedom beside the lake at Capernaum. Matthew tells how the collectors of the temple tax asked him whether his teacher paid it. Jesus asked him: from whom do kings take tax, from their sons or from others? From others, said Peter. Then the sons are free, Jesus answered; however, not to give offence, go to the sea, cast a hook, and in the first fish’s mouth you will find a coin; give it for me and for yourself (Matthew 17:24–27). There is verse 16 in a story: the Son of the King, owing nothing, paying anyway so as not to be a stumbling block, and including Peter in his freedom. Christians submit as free sons, and the Son pays their way.

Honor everyone. Universal, and it comes first: every human being, made in God’s image, including slaves, pagans and slandering neighbours. In a rigidly stratified society that was close to revolutionary.

Love the brotherhood. A narrower circle and a warmer word: respect for all, love for the family. Then fear God, which belongs to one being only (Proverbs 1:7).

Honor the emperor. The emperor gets the same verb as everyone, honour, the identical word as the first command, and he does not get the verb reserved for God. In a world where emperors were being called divine and incense was burned to them, that is a carefully calibrated sentence. Christians would not offer incense to the emperor as a god, but they would respect him as a ruler. Caesar is worth exactly as much honour as the man who cleans his stables, and not one degree of the fear that belongs to God. My son, fear the LORD and the king (Proverbs 24:21); render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s (Matthew 22:21).

How can I honour someone I find contemptible? By remembering that honour is given because of what a person is before God, not because of how he behaves. Every human being bears God’s image, however defaced, and every ruler holds an office God has made. You can disagree firmly, oppose a policy, even refuse an unjust order, and still refuse to mock, sneer or dehumanise. Honour looks like courtesy in speech, fairness in description, prayer for the person, and a refusal to rejoice in his downfall. If Peter could honour Nero, we can honour our opponents.

On a Tuesday. Ask the opposite question to honour: is there anyone you fear more than God? That fear is the one that makes you less free, and the Son has already paid your way.

verseByVerse.quote: Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust. For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? But if when you do good and suffer for it you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Servants, be subject. These were household slaves, not employees, and a large part of the population of those cities was enslaved; many early believers were slaves (see also 1 Timothy 6:1–2). Respect is literally fear, very probably reverence towards God shown in how they serve.

Peter speaks to slaves. Peter speaks to slaves directly, as moral agents with choices to make. Greek and Roman household codes did not normally do that; slaves were property, and you addressed their owners. Aristotle called a slave a living tool. The mere fact of the sentence assumes a dignity the culture denied. And note what is not here. Peter gives no corresponding instruction to masters, as Paul does (Ephesians 6:9), perhaps because few masters belonged to these congregations, or because his concern here is suffering under unjust authority. He is writing to the bottom of the ladder, and he gives the bottom of the ladder the longest passage in the chapter and the fullest picture of Christ.

Also to the unjust. Unjust, skoliois, is crooked, harsh (our word scoliosis). The household slave had no appeal against such a master, and Peter does not pretend otherwise.

For this is a gracious thing. Literally this is grace: something of God’s own favour is present in that endurance.

Mindful of God. The qualifier is essential. Mindful of God, dia syneidēsin theou, means because of conscience towards God, being conscious of God. What makes it grace is not the suffering, which by itself is merely misfortune, but that the sufferer is thinking about God while it happens. Endures, hypopherei, means bears up under. Sorrows, lypas, are pains and griefs, and unjustly, adikōs, is undeservedly. Peter is not commending endurance as a virtue in the abstract; he is describing a person who takes the injustice and holds God in view through it.

For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? Credit, kleos, is glory, fame, praise. Beaten, kolaphizomenoi, means struck with the fist, buffeted, the word used of the blows Jesus received in the high priest’s house (Matthew 26:67). The distinction is drawn sharply, and it protects the teaching from being sentimental. Deserved trouble borne quietly is not a spiritual achievement. Enduring deserved punishment earns no praise. The grace is in the undeserved kind.

In the sight of God. The master may never notice, but the slave’s patience is seen in heaven.

Does this mean the Bible approves of slavery? Peter addresses believers as they actually were, without endorsing the system. Scripture lays the seeds of its overthrow: a slave is a beloved brother (Philemon 16), Paul urges slaves to gain freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21), and he lists enslavers among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). Every human being is made in God’s image, and slave and master stand equal before Christ (Galatians 3:28). Christians, reading their Bibles, led many of the campaigns that ended the slave trade. It must be said honestly that other professing Christians defended slavery from the same Bible; but the slavery of the Americas was built on kidnapping, the very man-stealing the law punished with death (Exodus 21:16), and Peter’s words give it no cover.

And must a Christian employee today simply endure abuse? A modern employee is not a slave; he can leave, seek protection under the law and report wrongdoing. Peter’s principle still applies: do your work well and honour those over you, even when they are unfair, and do not repay evil with evil. But nothing here requires anyone to stay in an abusive situation or to cover up a crime.

What if I am being harmed at home? Then hear this clearly: this passage is not a command to stay in danger. Peter is addressing slaves who had no legal way out; you are not in that position, and the apostles themselves used the protection of the law (Acts 16:37). Abuse is a sin that God hates, and the church must never tolerate it or counsel anyone to endure it silently. Tell someone you trust, contact your church leaders and, if you are at risk, the police or an abuse support service. Seeking safety is not a failure of faith. What Peter forbids is revenge, not protection.

On a Tuesday. If you face unfair treatment at work this week, ask before you react: am I mindful of God right now? And be honest about the other half of Peter’s distinction: if the trouble is my own fault, I need to repent, not to feel noble.

For worship. God sent his Son in the form of a slave (Philippians 2:7), to be struck with fists and crucified by the death reserved for slaves. The Lord of glory took the lowest place, and so the lowest place is now holy ground.

verseByVerse.quote: For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For to this you have been called. This is a hard sentence, and it needs care. Called, eklēthēte: God’s effectual call (1:15; 2:9). To this: to patient endurance of unjust suffering. Peter does not say suffering is inevitable, or that God will bring good out of it, though both are true elsewhere. He says it is what they were called to, using the same word he has used of their calling out of darkness into marvellous light (2:9). One calling, two faces. Suffering is part of the Christian calling: it has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer for his sake (Philippians 1:29; 2 Timothy 3:12).

Because Christ also suffered for you. For you: in our place, before it was anything else. A servant who suffers unjustly is walking where his Lord walked.

Leaving you an example. The word for example is hypogrammos, and it is beautifully concrete. It is the schoolmaster’s copybook line: the letters written at the top of the page for a child to trace underneath. A teacher would write the letters perfectly; the student, tongue between his teeth, traced them below, line after line, wobbling, until his hand learned the shape. Peter’s picture of discipleship is a child’s hand moving over the master’s letters. Christ wrote the pattern; we trace it.

In his steps. Follow, epakolouthēsēte, means follow closely, and steps, ichnesin, are footprints, tracks. It keeps the same idea: footprints to be trodden in, one at a time. Walk exactly where he walked, placing your feet in his footprints, the way a child walks behind his father in deep snow. And Peter, of all people, chose that image. He is the man who said he would follow to prison and to death, and did not, and whose restoration on the beach ended with two words: follow me (John 21:19). He knows exactly how hard tracing those letters is, and he is writing to slaves rather than to apostles.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ is only an example. His death was first a substitution (v. 24), which no one can imitate. But having been saved by his substitution, we follow his example.

Why would God call anyone to suffer? Because he is making us like his Son, and his Son’s way to glory went through the cross (1:11; Hebrews 12:2). Suffering for doing good shows the world what Christ is like, refines faith (1:7), loosens our grip on this world, and prepares a weight of glory beyond comparison (2 Corinthians 4:17). God does not call us to suffer because he is careless of our pain, but because he has a purpose in it that is bigger than our comfort. And he does not call us to anything he has not done first. The footprints in front of you were made by bleeding feet.

On a Tuesday. Before you meet the hardest person of your day, picture the copybook: Christ’s letters at the top, your hand underneath. Trace one letter: a gentle answer, a silence instead of a retort. You will wobble. Trace it again tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He committed no sin. What follows is one of the most sustained meditations on Isaiah 53 in the New Testament, and Peter applies it, astonishingly, as workplace instruction for slaves. The words are Isaiah 53:9 almost verbatim. And Peter is not repeating a doctrine he has read. He knew Jesus personally for some three years, ate with him, travelled the roads with him, saw him tired, hungry, angry and grieved, and testifies that in all of it he found no sin (Hebrews 4:15; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 John 3:5). His suffering was entirely unjust.

No deceit. A slave suffering unjustly is tempted to retaliation and to the small deceits by which the powerless survive. Jesus did not lie his way out of a trial that would kill him.

He did not revile in return. Peter is describing something he witnessed, at least in part. Reviled, loidoroumenos, is insulted, verbally abused. At his trial and on the cross he was mocked, spat on, blindfolded and struck, and told to prophesy who hit him (Matthew 26:67–68; 27:39–44). He did not answer insult with insult. Peter was in the courtyard that night, near enough to see and hear (Luke 22:54–62). The imperfect tenses in Greek suggest sustained action: it kept coming, and the silence kept holding.

When he suffered, he did not threaten. A threat is the last weapon of somebody who has run out of others, and Christ was not out of options: twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53). Instead he prayed, Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34; some early manuscripts lack this prayer, though most modern Bibles keep it). Peter had drawn a sword in the garden; he learned from his Master’s silence what courage really was.

Continued entrusting himself. The whole passage turns on this. The verb, paredidou, means to hand over, to deposit, and it is imperfect: kept handing over, again and again, through the trial and the flogging and the nails. His last words were the same act: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! (Luke 23:46). And that is the mechanism, which the passage would be cruel without. He was not suppressing the desire for justice; he was transferring it. The case was not dropped; it was handed to a Judge who would hear it properly. Which is precisely what a slave with no court can do, and it is why Peter can ask this of people with no other recourse. Never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Romans 12:19).

Does entrusting myself to God mean I must not want justice? No. Wanting justice is right; God wants it more than you do. What Peter forbids is taking vengeance into your own hands. Entrusting means placing the case, with all its pain, in the hands of the Judge who sees everything and will put every wrong right, either at the cross for those who repent or at the judgement for those who do not. That is what frees you from bitterness. You do not have to carry the grievance, nurse it or settle it. You hand it over, and when it comes back to your mind, you hand it over again.

Can I still speak up or report wrongdoing? Yes. Jesus himself asked the officer why he struck him (John 18:23), and Paul appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 22:25). Speaking the truth, reporting a crime, seeking protection, or using lawful complaint procedures is not revenge. The difference is in the heart and the method: justice sought through proper means, without hatred, and willing to leave the outcome with God, rather than insult answered with insult and harm answered with harm.

verseByVerse.quote: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He himself bore our sins. And here Peter steps decisively past example. Christ has been the pattern for four verses; now he does something no follower can imitate. He himself, autos, is emphatic: no one else. Bore, anēnenken, means carried up, took up, offered up, echoing Isaiah 53:4, 11–12, and it is the verb used in the Greek Old Testament for carrying a sacrifice up to the altar. He carried our sins and their penalty (Hebrews 9:28). This is substitutionary atonement: our sins were laid on him, and he bore the punishment we deserved (Isaiah 53:5–6).

In his body on the tree. In his body anchors it. Not a spiritual transaction conducted elsewhere but sins carried in a physical body, up a hill, on a specific afternoon. Tree, xylon, wood, is the cross, and it is not a poetic word for it. It is the term from Deuteronomy 21:23: a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God. Peter used the same phrase preaching in Acts (5:30; 10:39), and it is his settled way of saying that Christ went under the curse. Paul draws the same line from the same verse of Deuteronomy: the one hanged on the tree became a curse in our place, to buy us out from under the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13).

Die to sin, live to righteousness. Die to sin, tais hamartiais apogenomenoi, is literally having ceased to exist with respect to sins, having departed from them. Christ’s death breaks sin’s power over us; we are united with him in his death (Romans 6:2–11). Dying to sin is not ceasing to feel its pull; it is that sin is no longer his master: he can say no to it, and when he falls he does not belong to it any more (Romans 6:14). Live to righteousness: a new life of obedience. The substitution has a moral aim. He did not bear sins so that we could continue in them, and Peter has been arguing for two chapters that the atonement produces holiness rather than excusing its absence.

By his wounds. This is Isaiah 53:5, and the word for wounds, mōlōps, is singular in Greek: the welt, the bruise, the swollen mark left by a lash. Peter is writing to household slaves. Some of them may well have had such marks on their own backs, and he tells them that the marks on his are what healed them. Healed, iathēte, in context means spiritual healing from sin: verse 25 goes straight on to straying sheep returning. For a beaten slave the image would have gone in like a nail: he has been where you are, and his stripes did what yours never could.

Where Christians differ: does this verse promise physical healing now? Some teach that physical healing is guaranteed in the atonement, so that believers can claim it now by faith. This commentary’s view: In context, Peter speaks of healing from sin: we were straying, now we have returned; we have died to sin. Christ’s atonement does secure the ultimate healing of our bodies at the resurrection (Romans 8:23; 1 Corinthians 15:42–44), and God may heal in answer to prayer now (James 5:14–15). But physical healing is not guaranteed in this life; believers still get sick and die, and the apostles themselves left sick friends behind (2 Timothy 4:20). The healing promised now is the healing of the soul. Christians who pray boldly for healing are right to pray; the difference is only over whether healing is promised now, and a sick believer who is not healed has not failed in faith.

How can one man bear the sins of millions? Because of who he is. A mere man could at best die for his own sins. But Christ is the eternal Son of God made man, of infinite worth and dignity, so that his one sacrifice is of infinite value (1:19). And he was sinless, so he had no debt of his own to pay. The Father laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:6), and he bore it fully, so that God is just in forgiving everyone who trusts him (Romans 3:26). The question is not whether his death is enough, but whether you are resting on it.

Is it not unjust for God to punish an innocent man in place of the guilty? Had God seized an unwilling stranger and punished him for crimes that were nothing to do with him, it would be. That is not what happened. The one who bore our sins is God the Son himself, who came willingly, saying of his life, no one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). The Judge did not make a third party pay; he paid himself. And Christ did not die as an outsider but as the head of his people, united to them as a husband to his bride, so that what was theirs became his and what is his becomes theirs. The cross is not God being cruel to the innocent. It is the holy God carrying the cost of his own mercy.

If Christ bore my sins, why do I still feel guilty? Sometimes because there is a sin you have not yet confessed; then confess it, and you will be forgiven (1 John 1:9). But often believers feel guilty over sins Christ has already carried, because the conscience is slow to believe the gospel. Then the answer is not to do penance, but to look at the cross. Your sins were really borne, in his body, on the tree. God does not punish the same sin twice. When guilt returns over forgiven sin, answer it with this verse, out loud if necessary: he himself bore my sins.

verseByVerse.quote: For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Straying like sheep. Isaiah 53:6. Sheep do not run away deliberately. They drift, head down, one mouthful at a time, until they look up and the flock is gone.

But have now returned. Returned, epestraphēte, can be read as passive: you were turned back. That fits everything Peter has said about being caused to be born again (1:3) and called out of darkness (2:9). Sheep are not famous for finding their own way home. They returned because they were turned, by the Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the one that is lost until he finds it, and lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing (Luke 15:3–7). I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed (Ezekiel 34:16).

Shepherd and Overseer. Two titles, and both are chosen with care for these readers. Shepherd, poimēn, is the tender one, and it carries Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34 and John 10 with it: the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and Peter will call him the Chief Shepherd (5:4). Overseer is episkopos, the guardian, the one who watches over and cares for; the same word translated bishop when it names a church officer. Peter gives the title first to Christ, and he will call himself merely a fellow elder in chapter 5. Jesus is the true Overseer of his people, over all human overseers (5:2–4).

Peter had strayed. And few people in the New Testament had more reason to write this sentence than Peter. He had strayed himself, spectacularly and in public, and he had been turned back, by a look across a courtyard and a charcoal fire on a beach, where he was asked three times whether he loved his Lord and then told three times to feed the sheep (John 21:15–17). So the chapter that began with newborn infants craving milk ends with a shepherd who goes after strays. Both images are about being kept alive by someone else’s care, which is the only thing Peter has offered these people from the start.

What if I have wandered since I became a Christian? Then this verse is for you too. The Shepherd does not only fetch sheep once; he goes on watching over their souls, and he brings back his own when they stray. Peter wandered after some three years at Jesus’ side, and was restored. Do not stay away out of shame, as if you had to clean yourself up before coming home. Sheep are carried back, not marched. Confess where you have gone, turn back to him today, and find a faithful church where you can be shepherded. He has not stopped being the Overseer of your soul.

For worship. We were lost, grazing our way towards the cliff edge, and the Shepherd who is also the Lamb came looking. He carried us home on his shoulders, and now he watches over our souls; he never sleeps, never loses count. We are his because he came looking.
