4.title: Stewards of Grace: The Meaning of Suffering
4.overview: Chapter 4 returns to suffering in the light of the end: “The end of all things is at hand” (v. 7). The first half (vv. 1–11) shows how suffering settles a believer’s break with the old life, and how a church facing the end should live: clear-headed for prayer, loving earnestly, hospitable, and using every gift for others. The second half (vv. 12–19) speaks directly to the fiery trial, and ends with entrusting the soul to a faithful Creator.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Stewards of God's Varied Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ’s suffering settles a believer’s break with the old life, which old friends find strange. With the end near, Peter describes a church that prays, loves, welcomes and serves, so that God is glorified through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Stewards of God's Varied Grace

Suffering for Christ settles a believer's break with sin. Because the end is near, stay clear-headed for prayer, love earnestly, and use each gift to serve others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Neighbours were baffled when converts no longer joined them, and spoke against them.

Now: Love covers a multitude of sins: it does not pass offences around.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Christ suffered in the flesh, so believers arm themselves with the same mind and are finished with living for desire (vv. 1–2). Old friends slander them but will give account to the Judge; believers who have died live with God (vv. 3–6). With the end near: pray, love, welcome, and serve as stewards of grace (vv. 7–11). The fiery trial is a share in Christ’s sufferings; suffer as a Christian, never as a wrongdoer, and entrust yourself to a faithful Creator (vv. 12–19).

Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh. Therefore picks up 3:18: Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous. In the flesh, sarki: in his body, physically, to death. Peter turns back from Christ enthroned (3:22) to the road that led there, and tells his readers it is their road too.

Arm yourselves with the same way of thinking. Arm yourselves, hoplisasthe, is a soldier’s word: put on armour. And what Peter hands them is not a shield but a thought. Way of thinking, ennoia, is mindset, attitude, settled resolve. His attitude was willingness to suffer rather than sin, and to do God’s will at any cost. A Christian ambushed by suffering he did not expect is far more likely to collapse than one who decided in advance what it means. Peter is telling them to make the decision before the trial rather than during it. And the armour is not our resolve alone: the Spirit who raised Christ supplies the strength (Romans 8:11–13).

Ceased from sin. Read flatly it seems to say that suffering makes a person sinless, which is plainly untrue and contradicts the commands that follow. Two readings carry weight. It may refer to Christ himself: he suffered and is now done with sin, having dealt with it once for all (3:18). Or, more likely given the whoever, it describes what suffering does to a believer’s relationship with sin. The person who has made a decisive break with sin, embracing suffering for Christ rather than compromise, has thereby shown that sin no longer rules him (Romans 6:7). It may also allude to union with Christ’s death: having died with him, we are finished with sin as a master.

For the will of God. Verse 2 supports the second reading. Human passions, anthrōpōn epithymiais, are the desires of people, what everyone around you wants. The break is about direction, not perfection: we never live for God’s will flawlessly, but Christ did, all the way to the cross, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). Once you have lost something real for Christ, the appeal of what you gave up is permanently reduced: you have already found out what it was worth. That is not sinlessness. It is a man who has stopped negotiating.

What does arming myself look like in practice? It means settling now, in a calm hour, what you will do when obedience becomes costly, so that you are not deciding in the heat of the moment. Decide in advance that you will not lie for your employer, that you will not join the mockery of the colleague, that you will tell your family you are a Christian, that you would rather lose the deal than cut the corner. Think through what it might cost, and pray it through. Read the accounts of Christ’s passion until his mindset becomes familiar. Then, when the moment comes, you will find that the armour is already on.

verseByVerse.quote: For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The time that is past suffices. Suffices, arketos: is enough. Peter does not argue them out of their old habits; he simply says the account is closed. Gentiles here means pagans, unbelievers (2:12), and Peter’s readers were mostly former pagans. What the Gentiles want to do is the will of the culture, set against the will of God of verse 2.

Six words. Sensuality, aselgeiai: unrestrained immorality, shameless excess. Passions, epithymiai: lusts. Drunkenness, oinophlygiai: literally overflowing with wine. Orgies, kōmoi: carousing, wild revelry, drunken night processions often linked to Dionysus. Drinking parties, potoi: drinking bouts. Lawless idolatry, athemitoi eidōlolatriai: abominable, forbidden idolatry. Much of it was religious: the temple feasts of a Greek city and the banquets of the trade guilds, held in temple dining rooms in honour of the guild’s patron god, ran on exactly this, and the last item names what held the rest together. Nearly the whole list is social, things done in company, which is precisely why leaving it cost these people their friends, and often their livelihoods.

They are surprised. Surprised, xenizontai, means to be taken aback. The word is related to xenos, stranger: the Christians have become strangers in their own town. Their neighbours are genuinely puzzled: not offended on principle but bewildered that anyone would opt out, and Christians came to be seen as antisocial, odd, and disloyal to civic religion.

In the same flood of debauchery. Join, syntrechontōn, means rush along with. Flood, anachysis, is an outpouring, a torrent running out of its channel. Debauchery, asōtia, is wild living, the word Luke uses (in its adverb form) of the prodigal son, who squandered his property in reckless living (Luke 15:13). When everyone is being carried along by a current, the person standing still is not merely different; he is an implied criticism of everyone moving past him.

And they malign you. Malign, blasphēmountes: slander. They mocked the Christians, perhaps as killjoys, haters of humanity, or atheists; the Roman historian Tacitus could describe the Christians as hated for their abominations and convicted of hatred of the human race. The slander this letter addresses does not begin in theological objection. It begins in social withdrawal: you stopped coming, and the people you stopped coming to have drawn their own conclusions about why.

Ransomed from the futile ways. The break was not a matter of willpower. Peter told these readers that they were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from their forefathers with the precious blood of Christ (1:18–19). The current they once ran with was a slavery, and someone paid to get them out. And when the neighbours malign them for it, they walk where their Lord walked. He was called a glutton and a drunkard by people who could not tell eating with sinners from sinning with them (Matthew 11:19). The Christian maligned for standing still is being treated as his Master was.

Does this mean Christians should avoid social occasions with unbelievers altogether? No. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners (Luke 7:34), and Paul says we cannot leave the world (1 Corinthians 5:9–10). Peter warns against joining in the excesses: drunkenness, orgies, idolatry. A Christian may be at the party; he should not be part of what the party becomes.

How do I handle friends who mock me for not joining in? With good humour, honesty and kindness. You do not need to preach at them or explain yourself at length; a simple, cheerful I would rather not is often enough. Keep up the friendship in other ways: invite them for a meal, help them move house, be there when life goes wrong for them. They are often more watchful than they seem, and many who mock now will one day come to the one friend who did not join in. Do not be bitter if some drift away. And find Christian friends too, so that you are not standing in the current alone.

verseByVerse.quote: but they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will give account. Give account, apodōsousin logon, is a steward’s word. The answer to being maligned is not vindication now but a court later: the same move as 2:23, where Christ entrusted himself to the one who judges justly. The slanderers will answer to God. Ready, hetoimōs, is the sharp word: he is standing by, and the delay is patience rather than absence. Judge the living and the dead may refer to Christ or to God the Father, and Scripture says both; Peter himself had told Cornelius that Christ is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead (Acts 10:42; 2 Timothy 4:1). All people, whether alive at his return or already dead, will be judged.

Is a God who judges not at odds with a God of love? Only if love is indifferent to evil. A God who never judged would be telling every slandered Christian in Bithynia, every abused child and every murdered martyr that what was done to them did not matter. Love that is not angry at what destroys the beloved is not love at all. The Bible’s God is slow to anger and ready to judge, and those two belong together: his patience gives time to repent (2 Peter 3:9), and his judgement means no wrong is finally swept aside. And the Judge of the living and the dead is the one who was judged for sinners at the cross, so that all who come to him find the verdict already borne (Romans 8:1).

Even to those who are dead. Another genuinely disputed sentence. Those who are dead, nekrois: most likely Christians who heard the gospel while alive and have since died, by martyrdom or ordinary death. That was a live pastoral problem: believers had been dying, sometimes under persecution, and the obvious taunt from neighbours was that their faith had done them no good at all. Some in the churches may have wondered the same, as the Thessalonians had (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). Peter answers that the gospel was preached to them in life for this very purpose.

Judged in the flesh. Judged in the flesh, krithōsi sarki: they suffered physical death, the common judgement for sin (Romans 5:12), or condemnation by human courts, or both. The way people are, kata anthrōpous: in human eyes. It was not the last word.

Live in the spirit. Live in the spirit, zōsi pneumati: they are alive in God’s presence, awaiting the resurrection, the spirits of the righteous made perfect (Hebrews 12:23; Revelation 6:9–11). The way God does, kata theon: according to God, in God’s estimation. Human verdict: condemned and dead. God’s verdict: alive.

The shape of Christ’s own death. Verse 6 has the shape of Christ’s own death and vindication, in almost the words of 3:18. Christ, too, was judged in the flesh the way people are: condemned by a human court and executed as a criminal. And God reversed the verdict by raising him. The believers whom Bithynia buried are following their Lord down the same road and up out of it. That is why the Judge of the living and the dead is no terror to them: he has stood under the world’s sentence himself, and come out alive on the far side.

Where Christians differ: does this teach a second chance after death? Some read this verse, alongside 3:19, as teaching that the gospel is preached to the dead in the afterlife, giving them an opportunity to believe. This commentary’s view: The verb is past tense (was preached), and the most natural reading is that the gospel was preached to people while they were alive, who are now dead. Scripture consistently teaches that death fixes one’s destiny (Luke 16:26; Hebrews 9:27). There is no second chance after death. The verse comforts believers: those who died in Christ are not lost but live with God.

Does this offer a second chance after death? Some early writers read it as preaching to the dead in Hades; others link it to 3:19. The more likely reading is that the gospel was preached to believers while they were alive, who have since died; though they suffered judgement in the flesh, they live with God. Scripture offers no second chance after death (Hebrews 9:27). The alternative reading empties the urgency of the New Testament’s own preaching, and it is not needed, because the natural reading is both simpler and more comforting.

Where are Christians who have died, and what are they doing? With Christ, consciously, in joy. Paul says that to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). They are not asleep in the sense of unconscious, nor waiting in purgatory to be purified; Christ’s blood has already done that. They rest from their labours (Revelation 14:13), worship, and wait with longing for the resurrection of the body at Christ’s return, when they will come with him and we will be reunited (1 Thessalonians 4:14–17). Grieve for them, but not as those who have no hope.

verseByVerse.quote: The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The end of all things is at hand. The word for end is telos: not merely the stopping but the goal, the completion, the point everything has been heading for. Peter is not announcing that things will run out; he is saying they will arrive. At hand, ēngiken, has drawn near, as in James 5:8. The next great event in God’s plan is Christ’s return, which is always near: no date is given, and every generation must live ready.

Why near? And at hand has drawn a great deal of comment, since two thousand years have passed. The New Testament’s consistent posture is not a calculated date but a nearness that makes everything urgent. The last days began at Pentecost (Acts 2:17), and the gathering in of God’s people goes on until the last is in. Scripture does name things that will come first, such as the final rebellion and the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3), but they are no timetable to calculate, for that mystery of lawlessness is already at work (2 Thessalonians 2:7). Peter himself writes that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day (2 Peter 3:8), so near, for him, was never a date on a calendar. Near describes the nature of the whole age: we live on the edge of eternity, and the door could open in any generation, ours included.

Therefore be self-controlled. You might expect a call to dramatic action: wind up your affairs, gather on a hillside. Peter says: be self-controlled and sober-minded, and pray. Self-controlled, sōphronēsate, means be sensible, of sound mind: the word used of the man from whom Jesus drove the demons, found sitting, clothed and in his right mind (Mark 5:15). Not panicked or carried away by end-time speculation, but clear-headed.

And sober-minded. Sober-minded, nēpsate (1:13; 5:8): alert, unintoxicated, the opposite of the drunkenness of verse 3. Peter’s answer to eschatological urgency is a steady head.

For the sake of your prayers. The clear head is so that they can pray, because a mind that is agitated, frightened or intoxicated cannot. Jesus told his disciples to watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation (Mark 14:38), and Peter slept instead, and was asked, could you not watch with me one hour? (Matthew 26:40). Within hours he was denying him. He has learned what a sleeping mind costs, and he had seen the alternative: that night only one mind in the garden was clear, the mind of Jesus, who prayed his way to the end of his own road and then rose and said, the hour has come; rise, let us be going (Mark 14:41–42).

Should I try to work out when the end will come? No. Jesus said that concerning that day and hour no one knows (Matthew 24:36), and every generation that has tried to set dates has been embarrassed. Scripture does not teach a secret rapture (the idea that believers will be taken away unseen before a final tribulation); it teaches one visible return of Christ, in glory, to raise the dead, judge the world and make all things new (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). Many dear Christians do expect such a rapture, and they share our longing for his coming; this commentary reads being caught up to meet the Lord as part of his one public return, because Paul describes it with a shout, a trumpet and the dead rising. The right response is not speculation but readiness: a clear mind, a praying heart, a loving life. Live every day as if he might come today, and plan as if he might not come for a hundred years.

How do I clear my head to pray? Begin by noticing what is clogging it: worry, noise, screens, resentment, too much to do. Pray at a time and place where those can be shut out, even for ten minutes: before the phone is switched on, on a walk, in the car with the radio off. Write down the worries that crowd in, then hand each to God. Pray Scripture, which steadies the mind, especially the Psalms. And keep short accounts with God and with others, because unconfessed sin is the loudest distraction of all. A sober mind is not a blank mind; it is a mind turned towards God.

verseByVerse.quote: Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above all. Earnestly, ektenē (1:22): fervent love that does not slacken. Under persecution, the church must hold together in strong love.

Love covers. The phrase comes from Proverbs 10:12: hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses. Covers, kalyptei, must be read rightly. This is not concealment of wrongdoing, and it is not the covering that atones; only Christ’s blood does that. It means love does not spread things. It refuses to publish, to exaggerate, to relitigate, to keep the account open (1 Corinthians 13:5, 7). A congregation of perhaps a dozen households under persecution, meeting weekly in someone’s front room, will generate friction constantly; and the difference between a church that survives that and one that tears itself apart is whether small offences get covered or circulated.

Whose sin is covered. Peter knows where this love is learned. Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered, sang David (Psalm 32:1), and the Christian knows what his own covering cost: Christ himself bore our sins in his body on the tree (2:24). A man who has had a multitude of sins covered by that blood is the last man entitled to keep a ledger on his brother. The love that covers is the cross reproduced on a small scale: the forgiven passing on a little of what they have received in full.

Without grumbling. Hospitality, philoxenoi, love of strangers, was not optional. The church met in a home, and travelling believers needed lodging, since inns were expensive and disreputable: a costly burden borne by whoever had the largest room (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2). Which is why without grumbling, aneu gongysmou, is attached. Peter knows that the household hosting the church is the household most likely to resent it, and that the resentment will come out as muttering rather than refusal. The command is not to open your door; they were already doing that. It is to stop complaining about the cost of it.

Does love covers a multitude of sins mean we should keep quiet about serious sin, abuse or crime? No. Love overlooks many small offences and forgives readily. But serious or unrepentant sin is to be confronted (Matthew 18:15–17; Galatians 6:1), and abuse and crime must be reported to the proper authorities (Romans 13:4). Covering sin in love never means hiding harm from those who need protecting.

How do I know whether to overlook something or raise it? Ask a few questions. Is it a small irritation, a thoughtless word, a matter of personality or preference? Then cover it: forgive it, and do not mention it to others. Is it a pattern that is harming the person or others, a serious sin, or something that is damaging your relationship so that you cannot let it go? Then go to the person privately and gently (Matthew 18:15). Is anyone in danger, or has a crime been committed? Then it must be reported, at once. Love overlooks much but never covers what endangers the vulnerable. When in doubt, ask a wise elder.

What if hospitality is genuinely hard for me? Then start small and start honestly. Hospitality is not about a beautiful house or elaborate food; it is about opening your life to others. A cup of tea, soup and bread, an invitation to Sunday lunch with whatever you were already eating. If your home is not suitable, take someone out for coffee, or help someone else host. If you are exhausted, or ill, or caring for someone, God knows your limits; do what you can, gladly. And notice that Peter forbids the grumbling, not the tiredness. Ask God for a cheerful heart, and remember that some have entertained angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2).

For worship. The Son of God came into his own world as a stranger, with nowhere to lay his head; he lodged in borrowed rooms and ate at other men’s tables. And the homeless Guest is the great Host: he has made us welcome in his Father’s house, strangers and enemies as we were, gone ahead to prepare a place for us, and set a table where the cost of the meal was his own blood, and he has never once grumbled at it. Every opened door in his church is a small sign of that hospitality.

verseByVerse.quote: As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace: whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies—in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As each has received a gift. Each, hekastos: every member has been given something. Gift, charisma, is a grace-gift, as in Romans 12:6 and 1 Corinthians 12:4: given by God’s grace, not earned, and not chosen.

Use it to serve one another. Serve, diakonountes, from which deacon comes. The gift is not for the possessor; it arrives already assigned to others, which settles the question of what gifts are for before anyone can make them a measure of standing.

Stewards of varied grace. A steward, oikonomos, managed a household that belonged to someone else (Titus 1:7), and would be asked about it. We do not own our gifts; we manage them for God, and it is required of stewards that they be found faithful (1 Corinthians 4:2). And varied, poikilēs, is a lovely word: literally many-coloured, used of an embroidered cloth. It is the same word as the various trials of 1:6. God’s grace is as many-coloured as our trials, and for every shade of trouble there is a matching shade of grace. The congregation is a fabric of different colours, and a single-coloured church has lost something God intended to be seen.

Oracles of God. Peter divides all gifts into two: whoever speaks and whoever serves. Oracles, logia, are words, utterances of God (Romans 3:2). That is a weighty standard. Not that every Christian’s words are inspired, but that anyone speaking in the congregation, teaching, preaching, exhorting, should handle the responsibility as though delivering God’s own utterances: his word, not their opinions (2 Timothy 4:2).

The strength that God supplies. Supplies, chorēgei, is the choregos word: in Athens a wealthy citizen funded a festival chorus lavishly, and the word came to mean provide abundantly. Practical service, cooking, visiting, giving, administering, runs on God’s strength, not our reserves, and God is a generous sponsor.

Through Jesus Christ. The gifts come from Christ: grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift, says Paul of the ascended Lord (Ephesians 4:7–8). They are shaped like Christ, who spoke only what the Father gave him to say (John 12:49) and came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45). And the glory returns through Christ, since our spiritual sacrifices are acceptable to God only through Jesus Christ (2:5). He is the way the gifts come down and the way the praise goes up.

Glory and dominion. Peter breaks into doxology mid-letter: a man thinking about gifts rightly ends up talking about God rather than about gifts. Him may be God or Christ; the grammar allows either, and either way all glory is his. Dominion, kratos, is might, the power to rule. The scattered, powerless congregations are reminded that the one they serve holds all power for ever.

Does whoever speaks include prophecy and tongues today? Peter divides the gifts into speaking and serving, and the speaking he has in mind is the church’s teaching, preaching and exhortation, handled as God’s word, not new revelation. Continuationists (Christians who believe that all the gifts of the apostolic age continue today) include prophecy here, and they are brothers and sisters whose love for Christ we gladly recognise; the more likely reading is that those who speak in the church today speak as one who speaks oracles of God by faithfully passing on the words God has already given. The revelatory gifts served to lay the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), and with the canon complete, Scripture is sufficient.

How do I find out what my gift is? Not mainly by taking a test, but by serving. Look at the needs around you in your church and start meeting them. Over time you will find what you do well, what others are blessed by, and what you find yourself drawn to. Ask mature Christians who know you what they see in you. Do not despise ordinary gifts: Peter puts serving beside speaking, and the person who stacks chairs, keeps accounts or visits the sick is as much a steward of God’s grace as the preacher. And remember that your gift is not your identity; it is God’s grace, lent to you, for others.

On a Tuesday. Before you serve someone this week, pray: Lord, supply the strength. Afterwards, say: to you be the glory. And if you have been holding back, waiting to be asked or to feel ready, step forward. The servant who buried his talent did so because he thought his master hard (Matthew 25:24–25); yours is the generous God who supplies.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter now speaks as though the fire has come, and tells his readers how to read it: as a share in Christ’s sufferings, a place where the Spirit of glory rests, and the start of God’s refining of his own house. It ends in trust in a faithful Creator.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgement Beginning at Home

Do not be surprised by the fiery trial. To suffer as a Christian is no shame; entrust your soul to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Christian” was probably an outsiders’ insult, and Peter told them to wear it.

Now: The name Christ gave us is worth bearing; let any suffering be for that name, not for wrongdoing or interfering.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, do not be surprised. The word for surprised, xenizesthe, think it strange, is the one used in verse 4 of the pagans. Peter turns it round: they are astonished at you; do not you be astonished at this. The fiery trial, pyrōsis, is literally the burning, the smelting furnace. Nero would soon burn Christians in Rome as living torches (AD 64); in Asia Minor the fire was probably not yet literal, and what felt like burning was the refiner’s furnace of 1:7, where faith is refined like gold.

To test you. When it comes, not if. To test you, pros peirasmon, names the purpose. A trial with a purpose is a different experience from a trial without one, though the heat is identical.

Something strange. The danger is not only the suffering but the interpretation: the conclusion that this is abnormal, that it means God has withdrawn, that other Christians somewhere are having an easier time and must be doing it better. Peter’s answer is that persecution is not a deviation from the Christian life but a normal feature of it. If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you (John 15:18–20; 2 Timothy 3:12). A hard word and a freeing one: a great deal of the pain of suffering is the suspicion that it should not be happening.

Insofar as you share. Peter is not commanding joy in suffering generally, but in the portion that is genuinely a share in Christ’s. Share, koinōneite, is the fellowship word: participation, not imitation (Philippians 3:10; Colossians 1:24). Not adding to his atonement, which is complete, but sharing in the opposition the world gave him. The hostility aimed at him in Jerusalem is now aimed at his body in Bithynia, and when his people bear it, they are standing with him. Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4).

When his glory is revealed. One joy, arriving in two instalments, and the second verb is the exuberant one: be glad, agalliōmenoi, exult, leap for joy (1:6, 8). The pattern: suffering, then glory (1:11; Romans 8:17). Peter had seen it once already, on a high mountain, when the face of his Lord shone like the sun (Matthew 17:1–2; 2 Peter 1:16–18); and he knew the glory that was coming was real.

How can I rejoice when I am suffering? Not by pretending it does not hurt, but by looking past the pain to what it means and where it leads. You rejoice that you belong to Christ so truly that the world treats you as it treated him; that the Spirit rests on you (v. 14); that your faith is being refined; and that the glory coming is beyond all comparison (Romans 8:18). The apostles left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41). You may weep and rejoice in the same hour. Joy here is not a feeling you produce, but a confidence God gives as you keep your eyes on Christ.

Should I expect persecution if I live faithfully? Yes, in some form, though its shape varies enormously. For some believers today it means prison, beatings, the loss of home or life; for others, mockery, exclusion, a career closed off, family rejection. Paul says all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12). Do not seek it, and do not provoke it by foolishness (v. 15). But do not be surprised by it, and do not conclude that God has abandoned you when it comes. And pray for the persecuted church around the world, which is bearing the fiery trial in its full heat today.

verseByVerse.quote: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Insulted for the name. Insulted, oneidizesthe, reviled, for the name of Christ: because you belong to him, not for being tactless (v. 15). Not imprisonment at this stage, but the daily contempt of neighbours, which is what most Christians under pressure actually face: not a courtroom but a reputation quietly destroyed.

You are blessed. The Beatitude again, as in 3:14: blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account (Matthew 5:11–12). Peter keeps returning to a sermon he heard on a hillside.

The Spirit of glory. The Spirit of glory and of God is the Holy Spirit, who brings God’s glory with him. The verb rests, anapauetai, is the one used in Isaiah 11:2, where the Spirit of the LORD rests on the shoot from the stump of Jesse: a messianic text. Peter says the same Spirit who rested on the Messiah settles on an insulted congregation in Bithynia. And there is very likely an echo of the glory cloud that rested on the tabernacle, when the glory of the LORD filled it and Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:34–35). The presence that filled the tent now rests on people being sworn at in the street, like Stephen, whose face shone like the face of an angel as they gnashed their teeth at him, and who saw the glory of God (Acts 6:15; 7:55). The visible shame is the outward face of an invisible glory: the Spirit rests on them precisely there.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add: on their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified. The earliest manuscripts lack it, so most modern Bibles omit it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only persecuted believers have the Spirit. All believers have him (Romans 8:9). It means that in persecution the Spirit’s presence is specially manifest and real.

How can I know the Spirit is resting on me when I feel nothing but humiliation? Peter does not say you will feel it; he says it is so. The Spirit’s presence is a fact grounded in God’s promise, not a sensation you must manufacture. Often believers who have suffered for Christ look back and see it: a strength they did not have, a peace that made no sense, words that came when they needed them (Matthew 10:19–20), a love for their enemies they could not explain. In the moment, trust the promise. The insult is real, but so is the glory, and only one of them will last.

For worship. The Spirit who hovered over the waters of creation, who filled the tabernacle with glory, who rested on Jesus at the Jordan like a dove, now rests on the mocked and the slandered people of Christ. The world sees only their disgrace; heaven sees the glory cloud settled over them. Glory to the Father who sends him, glory to the Son who poured him out, and glory to the Spirit who rests on the weakest saint as on a temple.

verseByVerse.quote: But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler. Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not as a murderer. The blessing of verse 14 is not for a Christian who has earned his trouble (2:20; 3:17). Evildoer, kakopoios, criminal, is the very accusation pagans were making against Christians (2:12). Do not prove them right.

Or as a meddler. Meddler, allotriepiskopos, is found nowhere earlier in Greek literature, and Peter may have coined it. It means an overseer of other people’s business: a busybody. Set beside murder and theft it is startling, because in a small suspected minority the busybody, tactlessly condemning pagan customs, does real damage. A Christian who cannot keep out of his neighbours’ business will generate hostility and then mistake it for persecution.

As a Christian. The word Christian appears only three times in the New Testament (Acts 11:26; 26:28; and here), and this is the only place where a believer takes it up as a name to be worn. It was coined at Antioch (Acts 11:26) and was almost certainly an outsiders’ nickname: Christ-people. Here it appears to be becoming a legal charge. Half a century later the governor Pliny asked the emperor whether Christians in Bithynia were to be punished for the name itself, even without any crime, and executed those who would not deny it.

Let him not be ashamed. Ashamed, aischynesthō. There is no shame in suffering for Christ: I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation (Romans 1:16; 2 Timothy 1:8, 12). The name is being thrown at them, and the instruction is to catch it. No one knew better than Peter what it was to be ashamed of the name: in a courtyard by a fire he had said, I do not know the man (Matthew 26:72).

Numbered with the transgressors. There is a deeper reason not to suffer as an evildoer: the cross. Christ was handed to Pilate with the words, if this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you (John 18:30). He was crucified between two robbers, and Jesus himself had said that the Scripture must be fulfilled in him: he was numbered with the transgressors (Luke 22:37; Isaiah 53:12). He bore the criminal’s name and the criminal’s death, though he committed no sin (2:22). To be a Christian is to carry the name of the Anointed One, who took the evildoer’s place; to earn the evildoer’s sentence by our own misconduct would be to turn his substitution into a joke.

In that name. The mockers supplied the word; the Christian makes it an occasion of praise, which takes the sting out of an insult more completely than any denial could.

How do I tell the difference between being persecuted and being a nuisance? Ask honestly what the people opposing you are objecting to. Is it your faith in Christ, your refusal to sin, your honest witness? Or is it your tone, your tactlessness, your habit of correcting everyone, your neglect of your work, your political rage dressed in Christian language? Ask a wise friend, because we are poor judges of ourselves. If you find you have brought the trouble on yourself, apologise and change; that is not compromise but humility. If after honest examination the offence is Christ himself, then stand firm and rejoice.

Does this mean I should keep my faith private to avoid trouble? No. Peter tells them not to be ashamed of the name, and to be ready to give an account of their hope (3:15). Keeping out of other people’s business is not the same as keeping quiet about Christ. You can speak of him openly, kindly and without apology, while refusing to be a busybody who polices your neighbours’ lives. The aim is that if you are opposed, it will be for the name, and for nothing else.
verseByVerse.note: “Christian” was first a nickname given by outsiders; it appears only three times in the New Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? And "If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?" Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The household of God. Time, kairos, is the appointed season. Household of God, oikou tou theou, is the church, God’s temple and family (2:5; 1 Timothy 3:15). The idea is Ezekiel’s. When judgement fell on Jerusalem, the command to the executioners was: begin at my sanctuary (Ezekiel 9:6), God’s own house first. And Malachi foretold that the Lord would come suddenly to his temple and sit as a refiner, purifying the sons of Levi (Malachi 3:1–5). The suffering of these congregations is not merely persecution from outside; it is the first movement of God’s own refining (v. 12). Their trials are not evidence of his absence. He has started, and he has started at home.

And if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? Outcome, telos, end. The argument runs from lesser to greater and Peter leaves it as a question, which is more forceful than a statement. If God’s refining is this painful for his own children, how terrible will his final judgement be for those who reject the gospel? They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:8–9). The reader is left to do the arithmetic about his persecutors, which is a far more sobering thing than being told. And note the phrase: those who do not obey the gospel. The gospel is not only an offer but a summons, and to refuse it is disobedience.

And if the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner? Verse 18 quotes Proverbs 11:31 as it stands in the Greek Old Testament. Scarcely, molis, means with difficulty. Not that salvation is uncertain or only barely achieved, nor that the righteous are saved by a narrow margin or barely enough grace. It means saved with difficulty: through fire, through great trial and suffering, through the process this letter has been describing. Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). Salvation is entirely secure, because God guards us (1:5), and the road to it is hard, and Peter has never pretended otherwise. If the righteous pass through such fire, what of the ungodly?

According to God’s will. Suffering is not outside God’s control (3:17). Not one of these sufferings has slipped past him.

A faithful Creator. The verb entrust, paratithesthōsan, is the deposit word: hand over for safekeeping, as valuables to a trusted friend before a journey. It is the word Jesus used on the cross: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! (Luke 23:46), echoing Psalm 31:5, where David prays: into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God. Peter takes both halves of that psalm verse, the committing and the faithful God, and puts them together. The title chosen for God is exact: Creator, ktistēs, used of him nowhere else in the New Testament. A man handing over his soul is giving it back to the one who made it, and faithful, pistos, means the deposit will be there when he asks for it. Paul could say: I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me (2 Timothy 1:12).

While doing good. The entrusting is done in the middle of acting, not instead of it. The hand that commits the soul to God goes on working for the neighbour.

Is God punishing me through my suffering? Not in the sense of making you pay for your sins, which Christ has fully paid. There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). But God does discipline his children, out of love, to make them holy (Hebrews 12:6, 10), and he uses suffering to refine and purify. So the question to ask is not, what is God making me pay for? but, what is my Father teaching me, and how can I grow? Sometimes suffering exposes a sin to turn from; often it is simply the road all his children walk. Either way, it comes from a Father’s hand, not a Judge’s sentence.

How do I actually entrust my soul to God? By handing over, in prayer, the things you cannot control: your life, your future, your reputation, the outcome of the trial, the people who are hurting you. Say it to him plainly, as Jesus did: into your hands. Remind yourself of who he is: your Creator, who made you and knows you, and faithful, who has never broken a promise. Then go on doing the good in front of you. When anxiety returns, entrust again. It is not a single act but a lifelong habit, and the dying Christ shows its last and greatest form.

Does this verse teach that hell is real and eternal? It points to it. If even the righteous pass through refining fire, the end of those who do not obey the gospel is far worse, and Scripture describes that end as conscious, eternal punishment, away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9; Matthew 25:46). Peter does not dwell on it, and nor should we with relish. But he does not soften it either, because only the truth about judgement makes sense of the urgency of the gospel and the wonder of grace. The fire that the ungodly will face is the fire Christ endured in the place of all who trust him.

On a Tuesday. Pray Jesus’ words over the thing you are most anxious about. Then do one good thing for someone else, right away, while the trouble is still unresolved. And pray for someone you know who does not obey the gospel; the question of verse 17 is meant to move us to plead with God, and with them.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin,<sup>2</sup>so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.<sup>3</sup>For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry.<sup>4</sup>With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you;<sup>5</sup>but they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead.<sup>6</sup>For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does.<sup>7</sup>The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers.<sup>8</sup>Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins.<sup>9</sup>Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.<sup>10</sup>As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace:<sup>11</sup>whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies—in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.<sup>12</sup>Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you.<sup>13</sup>But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.<sup>14</sup>If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.<sup>15</sup>But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler.<sup>16</sup>Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name.<sup>17</sup>For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God?<sup>18</sup>And "If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?"<sup>19</sup>Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.

5.title: Humble Yourselves: Elders, Community, and the God of All Grace
5.overview: Three movements: elders are to shepherd God’s flock (vv. 1–5); the whole church is to humble itself under God’s mighty hand, cast its anxieties on him and resist the devil (vv. 6–11); and closing greetings place the letter in “Babylon”, almost certainly Rome (vv. 12–14). It closes with a benediction for suffering people: after a little while, the God of all grace will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Shepherd the Flock of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes to the elders as a fellow elder, naming three temptations of leadership and the Chief Shepherd who is coming. Then he turns to the younger, and to everyone: put on humility, because God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble.
verseByVerse.theology:
Three Temptations and Their Remedies

Elders are to shepherd God’s flock willingly, eagerly and by example, not under compulsion, not for gain, not by domineering. The flock is not theirs, and its Owner is coming.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter wrote to elders as a fellow elder, not as an apostle.

Now: Everyone is to tie on the servant’s apron of humility.

verseByVerse.quote: So I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, as well as a partaker in the glory that is going to be revealed:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Peter, a fellow elder, urges the elders to shepherd God’s flock willingly, eagerly and by example; the Chief Shepherd will crown them (vv. 1–4). All clothe themselves with humility, casting their anxieties on the God who cares (vv. 5–7). Resist the prowling devil, firm in faith (vv. 8–9). After a little suffering the God of all grace will himself restore you (vv. 10–11). This is the true grace of God: stand firm in it (vv. 12–14).

So I exhort the elders. So, oun, therefore: because judgement begins at God’s household (4:17), its leaders must be faithful. Elders, presbyterous, plural: the leaders of each local church, also called overseers and shepherds (vv. 2–4; Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7). Every congregation has more than one, and a suffering flock needs faithful shepherds first.

As a fellow elder. Peter could have written as an apostle, and the letter opened that way (1:1). Here he sets the title down and takes the same chair as they. Fellow elder, sympresbyteros, appears nowhere else in the New Testament or in earlier Greek, so Peter may have coined it for this sentence: not authority over them but experience alongside them.

A witness. Witness, martys, the word that would come to mean martyr, as Peter himself became. He saw Jesus’ suffering firsthand: in Gethsemane, and from the courtyard where he failed. When he tells elders to shepherd the flock, the words come from a man who had denied he knew the Shepherd at all, and been given the sheep anyway.

A partaker in the glory. He was a witness of the sufferings; he is a partaker of a glory not yet revealed. Peter puts himself and them in the same position, between a suffering already seen and a glory still coming, which is where this whole letter has located its readers (4:13). He had seen glory once, on the mountain (Matthew 17:1–8), and wanted to stay; he writes as a man who knows the glory is real and that it is not yet time.

Where Christians differ: was Peter the first pope? Roman Catholic teaching holds that Christ made Peter head of the universal church, with authority passed to the bishops of Rome as his successors, reading Matthew 16:18–19 as founding a continuing office. Many devout Catholics hold this sincerely and love Christ; this commentary differs from them here with respect, because of what the texts themselves say. This commentary’s view: Peter calls himself a fellow elder, not a supreme pontiff. Christ is the Chief Shepherd (v. 4), the cornerstone (2:6), and the head of the church (Ephesians 1:22; Colossians 1:18). Peter was a leading apostle, the one God used to open the door of the gospel to Jews at Pentecost and to Gentiles at Cornelius’ house (Acts 2; 10), but the foundation of the church is the apostles and prophets together, with Christ as cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20), and Paul could rebuke Peter publicly (Galatians 2:11–14). The New Testament knows nothing of a papacy or of Peter’s authority being passed to Roman bishops. Local churches are led by a plurality of elders, under Christ.

Does Peter’s calling himself a fellow elder tell against the papacy? Roman Catholic teaching sees Peter as the first bishop of Rome with authority over the whole church (compare Matthew 16:18–19). Here Peter, writing probably from Rome (v. 13), places himself alongside the elders, not over them, and points them to Christ, the chief Shepherd. Nothing in his letters claims a supreme office or successors. Christians who order their churches differently, under bishops or under congregational rule, still agree that every church leader answers to the one Chief Shepherd.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for the elders of your church, one by one, and ask God to keep them humble, faithful and unafraid.

verseByVerse.quote: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not for shameful gain, but eagerly; not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shepherd the flock of God. Shepherd, poimanate, is the command Jesus gave Peter: tend my sheep (John 21:16), and now Peter passes it on. Shepherding includes feeding (teaching the word), leading, protecting from wolves, seeking the lost, binding up the injured and caring for the weak (Ezekiel 34:1–16). Christ is the Shepherd and Overseer (2:25), so these men are under-shepherds among a flock not theirs. It belongs to God because it was bought: Paul told the Ephesian elders to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood (Acts 20:28). Every elder handles sheep that cost the Son of God his life.

Exercising oversight. Episkopountes, from which bishop comes: elders and overseers are the same office (Acts 20:17, 28). Three pairs follow, each a temptation and its remedy, searching a leader’s motives.

Willingly. Under compulsion, anankastōs: reluctantly, because nobody else will, in a church where being an elder made you a target. As God would have you, kata theon, locates the willingness: not natural enthusiasm but a work taken up under God, from a heart that loves him and his people. The KJV lacks this phrase, following later manuscripts; several early ones have it, so most modern Bibles include it.

Not for shameful gain. Aischrokerdōs, in greed for shameful profit (Titus 1:7). Peter assumes elders could profit from the work, through the church’s support or through handling its funds, or the warning would be pointless. Elders may be paid (1 Timothy 5:17–18), but money must not be the motive. The alternative, prothymōs, eagerly, wholeheartedly, is the opposite of a man calculating what the post returns.

Not domineering. The third is power. Domineering, katakyrieuontes, is the very word the Lord used when he said the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, but it shall not be so among you (Mark 10:42–43). Peter was there, among the ten indignant at James and John, and heard the Lord finish: even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). The model for an elder is not the Gentile ruler but the ransoming Christ. Those in your charge, tōn klērōn, are the allotted ones: the people entrusted to each elder as a share is allotted, not owned.

But being examples. Examples, typoi, are patterns, the mark left by a seal (1 Timothy 4:12; Titus 2:7). Shepherds led their flocks rather than driving them (John 10:4), and this is not weak leadership but a costlier kind. A man who leads by command need only be obeyed; a man who leads by example has to be worth copying. No elder meets that standard without fault; the Chief Shepherd met it perfectly in his place, and that is why a failing shepherd can confess, be forgiven and go on.

What it does not mean. Not domineering does not mean elders have no authority. They lead and must be obeyed (v. 5; Hebrews 13:17). It means their authority is exercised humbly, by example, for the flock’s good.

What should a church member do if an elder is domineering or abusive? Speak to him first if it is safe, honestly and respectfully, as you would any brother (Matthew 18:15). If that fails or the matter is serious, take it to the other elders, who share responsibility for oversight; this is one reason the New Testament gives churches a plurality of elders. Paul says a charge against an elder should be received on the evidence of two or three witnesses, and that those who persist in sin should be rebuked publicly (1 Timothy 5:19–20). If there is abuse or a crime, it must be reported to the authorities. Elders are under-shepherds, not owners, and they answer to Christ and to the church.

On a Tuesday. Whatever leadership you have, in a home, a group or a workplace, ask which of Peter’s three temptations is closest: reluctance, money or power. Then, asking the Shepherd who lives in you by his Spirit for the gladness you lack, do the opposite once. And if you are not a leader, make your elders’ work a joy (Hebrews 13:17): thank one of them this week.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the chief Shepherd appears. Chief Shepherd, archipoimēn: Jesus Christ (2:25; John 10:11; Hebrews 13:20). The word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament: there is one Chief Shepherd, and every elder is under him. His appearing answers the three temptations at their root. A man who believes the flock belongs to someone else, who is coming back, will not serve grudgingly, or for money, or by domineering, because none of those makes sense if you are minding somebody else’s sheep and he is due home.

The unfading crown of glory. The crown is stephanos, the victor’s wreath at the games rather than a royal diadem: a circle of olive or pine leaves, and everyone knew how quickly it browned. Unfading, amarantinos, is from the amaranth, the flower the ancients used as a symbol of what does not wither (compare 1:4; 1 Corinthians 9:25). The crown of glory most likely means the crown that consists of glory, as the crown of life in James 1:12 means the crown which is life. The reward is not a decoration to wear but a share in the glory Peter has just said he is a partaker of.

A reward for the unseen. These elders’ work was often unpaid, unnoticed outside their own street, and dangerous. Peter tells them the recognition is coming from the only person whose opinion is final.

Is it right to serve God for a reward? Yes, if the reward is what God offers and the motive is love for him. Scripture repeatedly holds out reward as an encouragement (Matthew 6:4; Hebrews 11:6), and Jesus himself endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). What is wrong is serving for the wrong reward: money, praise, power, the admiration of the congregation. The crown of glory is not wages that put God in our debt; it is a gift of grace crowning the work grace produced. And the faithful will cast their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10), because the best part of the reward is the one who gives it.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders. Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, you who are younger. Peter turns to those most likely to chafe. Younger, neōteroi: younger people in the church, or perhaps a group of younger men who served the church practically, like the young men who carried out Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:6, 10). Elders probably means the office, continuing from verses 1–4. Be subject, hypotagēte, is the same word as 2:13, 18; 3:1: the posture the letter has asked of citizens, slaves and wives.

Clothe yourselves with humility. Then the scope widens: all of you, elders to members as much as members to elders. The verb, enkombōsasthe, means to tie on, as a servant’s work apron. Peter had seen it happen. In the upper room the Lord rose from supper, tied a towel round himself, and washed their feet, and Peter had objected, loudly, and been told: if I do not wash you, you have no share with me (John 13:4–17). The picture he reaches for here is one he originally refused.

God opposes the proud. The quotation is Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek form, as in James 4:6. The word for opposes, antitassetai, is military: to draw up in battle order against. God does not merely decline to help the proud; he takes the field opposite them. And grace, being a gift, can only be received by open hands, which is why humility is not one virtue among several here but the posture in which anything at all can be received.

What does humility actually look like? It looks like being willing to do the lowly job without being asked or thanked; listening more than speaking; admitting when you are wrong, quickly and without excuses; rejoicing when others are praised; asking for help; receiving correction without sulking; and thinking of yourself less, rather than thinking less of yourself. It is not putting yourself down, refusing compliments, or pretending you have no gifts. C. S. Lewis remarked that the humble man will not be thinking about humility at all, because he will not be thinking about himself. The root of it is seeing yourself rightly before God: a sinner saved by grace, with nothing you did not receive (1 Corinthians 4:7).

I am young and disagree with my church leaders. What should I do? Respect them, pray for them, and speak to them. Submission does not mean you must have no opinions, or that elders are never wrong. It means you approach them with humility rather than contempt, assume the best of their motives, ask questions before making accusations, and support their decisions where conscience allows, even when you would have done it differently. If a matter is serious, raise it privately and respectfully. Do not stir up a faction. And be willing to consider that age and experience may see what you do not yet see, just as you may see what they have missed.

On a Tuesday. The Lord tied on the towel and washed you first. When you are corrected this week, by a spouse, a boss, an elder or a child, try saying thank you before you say but.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Cast Your Anxieties, and Stand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole church is to humble itself under God’s hand, handing him its worries, and to stay alert against an enemy who hunts the isolated. Suffering is for a little while; the God of all grace will himself restore his people. Peter sums up his letter as the true grace of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why Worry Is Treated as Pride

Humble yourselves by casting all your anxieties on God, because he cares for you. After a little while, the God of all grace will himself restore you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The devil prowled like a roaring lion, looking for anyone cut off from the flock.

Now: Resist him, firm in the faith, knowing the same sufferings are shared by believers throughout the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under the mighty hand of God. Since that is how God deals with pride, put yourself on the right side of it. Humble yourselves, tapeinōthēte, is passive in form: be humbled, accept the humbling. The mighty hand of God is an exodus phrase: God brought Israel out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm (Exodus 3:19; 6:1; Deuteronomy 9:26). The hand that disciplines is the hand that delivers. Accept God’s dealings with you, including suffering, without resentment or resistance.

At the proper time. En kairō: God’s timing, not ours. A man who insists on being raised now has taken the job out of the right hands.

Under the mighty hand, to the right hand. Christ walked this verse first. He humbled himself to the point of death, and therefore God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:8–9). In Gethsemane he did not hide his anguish; he offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him (Hebrews 5:7), and then went under the mighty hand to the cross. At the proper time God lifted him, as Peter preached at Pentecost: exalted at the right hand of God (Acts 2:33). The road Peter commends to anxious believers runs from that garden to that throne, and they walk it in him.

Casting all your anxieties on him. The grammar matters. Casting is not a separate command; it is a participle attached to humble yourselves: the casting is how the humbling is done. We do not usually think of worry as pride. Peter sees a link: holding on to your anxieties can be a way of insisting that the situation is yours to manage, and handing them over is an act of self-lowering. This is not a rebuke to the anxious. Peter writes to frightened people, and he ends the sentence with he cares for you, so the call to humility comes as an open door, not a scolding. Casting, epiripsantes, is a decisive verb: throw it (Luke 19:35). It echoes Psalm 55:22: cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you. And all leaves no category too small to bother him with. Anxieties, merimna, is the word Jesus used when he said do not be anxious about your life (Matthew 6:25–34).

Because he cares for you. The ground of the whole thing is not that he is capable but that he is concerned. The word, melei, means it matters to him. There is a play of sound in Greek between our merimna and his melei: our care, his care. Peter is writing to people whose neighbours had decided they were nothing, and the last word of the sentence is that they are on somebody’s mind.

Is anxiety a sin? This verse is an invitation, not a rebuke: he cares for you. Anxiety rooted in pride is to be cast on God, but anxiety with bodily causes is an illness, and a doctor’s help is no lack of faith. (See 2 Corinthians 2:12 for the fuller answer.)

How do I actually cast my worries on God? Specifically and repeatedly. Name each worry to him in prayer, one by one, out loud or on paper: not a vague request for peace, but this diagnosis, this debt, this child, this meeting. Tell him what you fear will happen. Then deliberately hand it over: Father, this is yours; I cannot carry it. Do what is yours to do about it, and leave the rest. When the worry comes back, and it will, cast it again, without scolding yourself. Pair it with thanksgiving (Philippians 4:6–7), which reminds the heart of how often he has carried you before.

For worship. The hand that is mighty enough to part the sea is gentle enough to take our smallest care. He carried the whole weight of our sin on the cross, and he is not going to drop the lesser burdens now.

verseByVerse.quote: Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be sober-minded; be watchful. The first has appeared before (1:13; 4:7). The second, grēgorēsate, stay awake, is the word from Gethsemane: watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation (Matthew 26:41; Mark 14:37–38). Peter slept, and within hours had denied his Lord (Mark 14:66–72). He knows the cost of not being watchful.

Your adversary the devil. Adversary, antidikos, is a courtroom word: the opponent in a lawsuit, the prosecutor. Devil, diabolos, means slanderer. These readers were being accused, publicly and continuously. Satan accuses believers before God (Job 1–2; Zechariah 3:1; Revelation 12:10) and slanders them through human persecutors. He is real, personal and hostile.

Is belief in a personal devil not a relic of a superstitious age? It would be if the Bible pictured him as a horned figure behind every misfortune, but it does not. Scripture speaks of him soberly: a created being, a fallen angel, powerful but limited, already defeated, and working mostly through lies, accusation and fear (John 8:44). Many thoughtful people who have looked hard at the cruelty of the last century have found it difficult to explain by human weakness alone. And the denial suits him. A soldier who does not believe there is an enemy will not keep watch, which is exactly why Peter’s first words are be sober-minded; be watchful. The devil is not to be feared as God’s equal. He is to be taken seriously as God’s defeated rebel.

Like a roaring lion. Prowls, peripatei: the picture is hunting. In Scripture the lion’s roar is the sound of a terrifying enemy (Psalm 22:13; Ezekiel 22:25), and Peter’s point seems to be that this enemy works first on the nerves. The noise is meant to frighten before it wounds. Under Nero, within a few years, Christians in Rome were sewn into animal skins and torn by dogs.

Seeking someone to devour. Devour, katapiein, swallow up. The hunt is selective. He is looking for the one that has drifted from the group, the isolated, the weak, the careless, which is exactly what persecution does to a congregation.

Resist him, firm in your faith. Resist, antistēte, stand against (James 4:7): stand, not attack. Firm, stereoi: settled like a rock, the opposite of the scattering the roar is designed to produce. Resistance comes through faith, taking up the shield of faith (Ephesians 6:16), in the power of the Spirit rather than our own strength.

Sifted like wheat. Peter had been hunted before, and he knew who kept him. On the night of the betrayal Jesus said, Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:31–32). The lion found him by a charcoal fire, and he fell; but his faith did not fail, because Christ had prayed for it. So when Peter says resist, firm in your faith, the firmness is not the believer’s own grip. It is the faith Christ prays for, held by the Lord who answered the devil in the wilderness with the word of God (Matthew 4:1–11) and disarmed him at the cross (Colossians 2:15).

Your brotherhood throughout the world. Brotherhood, adelphotēs, as in 2:17. Not relief but company. Isolation is the lion’s method, and the answer is knowing you are one of many, which is why Peter wrote a circular letter to churches across five regions rather than a private note.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every difficulty is a direct satanic attack, or that we should be obsessed with the devil. He is a defeated enemy (3:22; Colossians 2:15).

How does the devil actually attack Christians today? Mostly not with dramatic manifestations, but with the same tactics Peter names: accusation, fear and isolation. He accuses, telling you that you are too sinful for God to forgive, or that your faith is fake. He frightens, making obedience look too costly. He isolates, drawing you away from church and Christian friends until you are alone. He also deceives, with false teaching and with temptations dressed as freedom. The answer is the same as Peter’s: stay awake, stay in the word, stay with the flock, and when he accuses, answer with the blood of Christ. He is a lion, but he is a lion on a chain.

verseByVerse.quote: And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After you have suffered a little while. The suffering stands, and it is bounded. A little while, oligon, is the same phrase as 1:6, measured against the eternal glory in the next clause (2 Corinthians 4:17).

The God of all grace. Not the God of all power, though he is, but of all grace: his goodness given freely to people who have earned the opposite, the many-coloured grace of 4:10. My grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9).

To his eternal glory in Christ. Called, kalesas: God’s effectual call, which does not merely invite but brings a person to faith (1:15; 2:9). The calling looks past the suffering to the destination, his own glory (Romans 8:30), the glory Peter said in verse 1 he is a partaker of. And in Christ gives the road its shape. The prophets foretold the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories (1:11), and the risen Lord asked, was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (Luke 24:26). Suffering, then glory, is first his story, and union with him makes it ours: we suffer a little while because he suffered once, and we will be glorified because he already is.

Restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish. Four verbs, and the emphatic word is himself, autos: God personally. Restore, katartisei, is the mending word, used of setting a bone and of mending nets (Mark 1:19), which Peter had done for a living. It assumes damage: the suffering will break something, and God will set it. Confirm, stērixei, to make firm, set fast, is the word the Lord used when he told Peter: when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers (Luke 22:32), and here Peter does just that. Establish, themeliōsei, is to lay on a foundation. Those God truly calls he keeps to the end: God will finish what he started (Philippians 1:6). And it comes from a man who had been broken and repaired by name.

To him be the dominion. The KJV reads glory and dominion, following later manuscripts that add glory; the earliest have dominion alone. Peter has just named the prowling lion; he ends by saying whose the dominion actually is. The devil roars, but God rules.

What it does not mean. It does not promise that suffering will end in this life. Restoration may be partial now and complete in glory. But it is certain.

What if I feel broken beyond repair? Then this verse was written for you. Peter promises that God will restore, and the word assumes real damage: a broken bone, a torn net. He does not say the breaking did not happen or did not matter. He says God himself will mend it. That mending may begin now, slowly, through his word, his people, prayer and time, and sometimes through doctors and counsellors he provides; and it will be complete when Christ appears. Peter had been broken by his own denial, and Christ restored him on a beach. The God of all grace has never yet met a soul too broken for him.

On a Tuesday. Pray this promise back to God, naming the broken thing. Then look for one person in your church who is broken by suffering, and be one of the hands God uses to strengthen them, as Peter was told to strengthen his brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him, I have written briefly to you, exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings, and so does Mark, my son. Greet one another with the kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By Silvanus. Silvanus is the Silas of Acts, Paul’s companion who sang hymns at midnight in the jail at Philippi (Acts 16:25), now carrying Peter’s letter. By, dia, through: he may have been Peter’s secretary, helping with the polished Greek of a Galilean fisherman, or the bearer of the letter, or both. That Paul’s companion helps Peter shows that the apostles were not rival parties.

I have written briefly. Five chapters, and a lifetime of experience compressed into them (compare Hebrews 13:22).

The true grace of God. Peter’s own summary: after five chapters on suffering, submission and slander, he calls the whole thing grace: not advice, not endurance training, but true grace, alēthē charin. And the grace has a name. The prophets, Peter wrote, spoke of the grace that was to be yours as they searched out the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow (1:10–11). The true grace of God is Christ himself, crucified and glorified, given to exiles.

Stand firm in it. The KJV reads wherein ye stand, a statement rather than a command, following later manuscripts; the earliest have the command. Not produce it, or earn it: stand in it, as a man stands on solid ground in an earthquake.

She who is at Babylon. She is almost certainly the church there, God’s chosen lady (2 John 1), and Babylon is very probably a code name for Rome, as in Revelation 14:8; 17:5; 18:2, not the largely deserted Mesopotamian city. Early tradition places Peter in Rome at the end of his life, where he was martyred under Nero. Calling the capital Babylon reminds them that the church at the centre of the world is as much in a foreign country as the church in Bithynia. And likewise chosen, syneklektē, chosen together with you, hands them back the word he opened with (1:1).

And so does Mark, my son. John Mark, who abandoned Paul and Barnabas on the first missionary journey (Acts 13:13), and was later restored, so that Paul could call him very useful to me for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). My son is affection, not paternity. Peter had gone to Mark’s mother’s house in Jerusalem when the angel freed him from prison, and found the church praying there (Acts 12:12). Early tradition, from Papias, says that Mark became Peter’s interpreter and wrote down in his Gospel what Peter preached. Two men who had both failed, both been restored, standing together at the end.

The kiss of love. A family greeting, used in the early church (Romans 16:16). Slave and master, Jew and Gentile, greeting each other as brother and sister. The letter that has spoken so much of hostility ends with an instruction to touch each other.

Peace to all of you who are in Christ. Peace, eirēnē, the Hebrew shalom, wholeness, offered to people who had very little of it, from a man who would shortly die in the city he calls Babylon. It was the first word the risen Lord spoke to the disciples gathered in the locked room: peace be with you (John 20:19). Peter ends where his Lord began.

Must Christians greet each other with a kiss today? What is commanded is warm, holy affection, in the form one’s culture uses for it. (See Romans 16:16 for the fuller answer.)

What does it mean to stand firm in grace? It means refusing to move off the ground God has put you on. Do not slide into earning your standing by performance, as though suffering meant you had not done enough. Do not slide into despair, as though suffering meant grace had failed. Do not slide into compromise, as though grace could be kept while denying Christ. Stand on what this letter has told you: you are chosen, born again, ransomed, guarded, loved, called to glory. Keep coming back to it in the word, at the Lord’s Table, among his people. Grace is not only how you began; it is where you stand every day until he comes.

On a Tuesday. Read 1 Peter through in one sitting this week; it takes about twenty minutes. Then write one sentence on what the true grace of God means for your life right now.

For worship. This is the true grace of God: that the Father chose exiles, the Spirit set them apart, the Son ransomed them with his blood; that he caused them to be born again to a living hope, guarded them by his power, refined them in the fire, and called them to his eternal glory. It is grace that holds in Babylon and Bithynia, that turned a denier into an apostle and a deserter into an evangelist. And over every scattered, slandered, suffering child of God, the last word is his: peace, in Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Silvanus is the Silas of Acts. “Babylon” is very probably a code name for Rome. Mark is John Mark, whom early tradition links with Peter as the source of Mark’s Gospel.
